title: Evaluate the suitability of beef carcasses and organs for human consumption

lessons.title: Identifying abnormalities in beef carcasses
lessons.html:
The task

Every bovine carcass, with its head and organs, must be examined and judged before it may be sold. The meat examiner works under the Meat Safety Act 40 of 2000 and its regulations, within the limits of their authority, and refers difficult or serious cases to the meat inspector or veterinarian.

Sources of information

  • Ante-mortem: lameness, fever, recumbency, emaciation, emergency slaughter, signs of nervous disease.
  • Post-mortem: systematic examination of head, tongue, pluck, liver, viscera, and carcass with observation, palpation and prescribed incisions.
  • Carcass state: bleeding, setting, colour, smell, fat colour (yellow fat can be normal in older grass-fed cattle and must be distinguished from jaundice).

Common deviations in cattle

FindingTypical sites
Bovine measles (Cysticercus bovis)Cysts in masseters, heart, tongue, diaphragm and other muscles; larva of Taenia saginata, a human tapeworm
TuberculosisCaseous or calcified lesions in lymph nodes of head and lungs, lungs, and sometimes other organs
Liver flukeThickened, calcified bile ducts
Hydatid cystsLiver and lungs
Liver abscessesCommon in feedlot cattle
Pneumonia, pleurisy, pericarditisLungs, chest wall, heart sac (traumatic pericarditis from swallowed wire)
BruisingHips, shoulders, ribs from transport and handling
Jaundice, oedema, emaciationWhole carcass
Septicaemia and pyaemiaHaemorrhages, congestion, multiple abscesses, enlarged lymph nodes
ContaminationHide, hair, ingesta, faeces, milk from the udder

Key question: is the lesion localised or is there evidence of generalisation such as several affected lymph nodes in different body regions, fever signs, or multiple lesion sites?

Controlled diseases

Some findings, such as signs suggesting anthrax, tuberculosis or other controlled diseases under the Animal Diseases Act 35 of 1984, require immediate detention and referral. Suspected anthrax carcasses must not be opened further.

lessons.title: Formulating and executing the judgement
lessons.html:
Judgement categories

  • Passed fit for human consumption.
  • Passed after removal of affected parts.
  • Passed conditionally, where the regulations allow treatment such as freezing for certain light infestations; such treatment is only applied as the regulations and the inspector direct.
  • Detained pending further examination or tests.
  • Totally condemned.

Applying principles to beef

SituationDirection of judgement
Bruise on the hip, carcass normalTrim bruised tissue; pass carcass
Liver abscesses, carcass normalCondemn liver; pass carcass
Single measles cyst foundDetain; further incisions to determine degree of infestation; judgement according to the regulations
Heavy measles infestationTotal condemnation according to the regulations
Tuberculous lesionsDetain and refer; judgement depends on whether lesions are localised or generalised
Traumatic pericarditis with septic signsUsually total condemnation; refer
Generalised jaundice or oedemaDetain, refer, usually condemn

Executing the judgement

  1. Communicate the decision clearly to the line and the detain rail operator.
  2. Ensure all affected parts are removed and placed in condemned containers.
  3. Keep detained carcasses with all their parts, under tag, in the detention area.
  4. Check that condemned carcasses are marked and moved to the condemned room.
  5. Sterilise all instruments that contacted lesions.

Judgements must be consistent and defensible. Owners may question a condemnation, so findings and reasons must be clear and recorded.

lessons.title: Completing the task
lessons.html:
Marking

The approved inspection mark is applied only to passed carcasses and parts, by authorised people. Detention tags stay on detained carcasses until a final decision. Inspection stamps are stored securely.

Condemned material

  • Held in leak-proof, marked containers in a lockable condemned room.
  • Disposed of by an approved method.
  • Never released to staff, the public or animal feed outside approved routes.

Records and reporting

  • Daily slaughter numbers by owner.
  • Conditions found, parts or carcasses condemned, and reasons, by carcass number.
  • Outcome of detentions, laboratory results and conditional approvals.
  • Immediate reporting of suspected controlled diseases to the veterinarian.

Abattoir findings contribute to national disease surveillance. For example, measles detection can be traced back to the farm so the source of human tapeworm contamination can be addressed.

Feedback

  • To the producer: liver fluke and measles rates, bruising patterns pointing to rough handling or transport problems.
  • To the line: contamination and dressing faults, so they are corrected quickly.

Safety

Several bovine conditions, including tuberculosis, anthrax and brucellosis, can infect people. Wear the required PPE, cover wounds, sterilise instruments, and report illness. Suspected anthrax requires immediate stop and referral.

Key points

  • Combine ante-mortem and post-mortem findings in every judgement.
  • Distinguish localised lesions from generalised disease.
  • Measles, tuberculosis and other zoonoses require detention and judgement according to the regulations.
  • Do not open suspected anthrax carcasses; refer immediately.
  • Mark, secure and record every decision clearly.
